title: C++ Programming Foundations

target.learner: A tertiary fresher or independent beginner with basic computer literacy and no assumed programming experience
target.professionalOutcome: Write, compile, debug, verify, document, and publish small modern C++20 programs using safe value ownership and the standard library, with enough fluency for introductory practical examinations and beginner projects.

assumptions: The learner has a Windows computer and basic file, browser, and typing skills.
No prior programming, terminal, Git, C, C++, compiler, debugger, testing, object-oriented, or memory-management knowledge is assumed.
Setup is separate from the eight instructional Weeks and may be skipped capability by capability after verification.
Required learning resources are free to access; a free verified GitHub account is needed only for final repository publication.
Most project work can continue offline after the required tools and referenced materials have been opened or downloaded.
This course teaches a modern standard-library-first subset of C++20 and deliberately excludes raw ownership, manual allocation, advanced templates, concurrency, and production security claims.

phases.title: Run and Reason with Modern C++
phases.outcome: Build a correct mental model of C++20 execution, typed values, complete-line input, validation, iteration, vectors, and safe summaries.

phases.title: Organize Owned Values and Dependable Behavior
phases.outcome: Use functions, const references, multi-file interfaces, classes, RAII, algorithms, maps, file streams, debugging, and checks to create dependable small programs.

phases.title: Integrate, Verify, and Share
phases.outcome: Assemble, document, inspect, and publish a reproducible modern C++ command-line project for human review.

competencies.name: Verify a Windows C++ workspace
competencies.description: Open a C++ project in VS Code, verify the intended GCC and GDB executables, compile a saved C++20 source file with warnings enabled, and run the resulting executable from PowerShell.

competencies.name: Explain how C++ source becomes a running program
competencies.description: Distinguish source, preprocessing, compilation, linking, an executable, and process output at beginner depth.

competencies.name: Read and repair early C++ diagnostics
competencies.description: Use diagnostic severity, source location, and the first relevant compiler or linker message to repair one cause without guessing.

competencies.name: Represent and display typed C++ values
competencies.description: Create initialized int, double, bool, char, and std::string values and produce readable labelled output with std::cout.

competencies.name: Read complete console lines
competencies.description: Use std::getline for text input, preserve spaces deliberately, and distinguish an empty line from a stream failure.

competencies.name: Parse numeric text with full validation
competencies.description: Convert a complete input line to a number, reject trailing text and out-of-range values, and keep failed input from changing valid state.

competencies.name: Express ordered decisions
competencies.description: Use comparisons, short-circuit Boolean operators, and ordered if/else-if/else branches so invalid, boundary, and successful cases take one explainable path.

competencies.name: Repeat work with a visible stopping rule
competencies.description: Use for and while loops with intentional starting state, progress, and termination, then trace changing values without guessing.

competencies.name: Manage an ordered std::vector
competencies.description: Add, inspect, traverse, and query values in a vector while distinguishing size from the last valid index.

competencies.name: Summarize a collection safely
competencies.description: Compute count, total, average, minimum, maximum, and threshold results while handling an empty vector before dependent operations.

competencies.name: Define focused functions
competencies.description: Write functions with purposeful names, explicit parameter and return types, and one understandable responsibility.

competencies.name: Choose value and const-reference parameters
competencies.description: Pass small values by value, read larger objects through const references, return owned results by value, and avoid dangling references.

competencies.name: Build a namespaced multi-file program
competencies.description: Place declarations in guarded headers, definitions in source files, use a small namespace, compile every translation unit, and distinguish compiler from linker failures.

competencies.name: Construct valid class objects
competencies.description: Define a class with private fields and a constructor that establishes one valid object from its first observable state.

competencies.name: Protect invariants through member functions
competencies.description: Expose const observations and validated commands so an object rejects invalid state transitions before mutation.

competencies.name: Reason about value ownership and RAII
competencies.description: Explain object lifetime, automatic cleanup, copy independence, and why standard-library values remove the need for beginner manual memory management.

competencies.name: Apply standard algorithms to ranges
competencies.description: Use find_if, count_if, sort, and transform with valid iterator ranges rather than rewriting every traversal by hand.

competencies.name: Write narrow lambdas with explicit capture
competencies.description: Use short predicates and projections whose parameters, return behavior, and captured values are visible and intentional.

competencies.name: Use associative containers for keyed summaries
competencies.description: Store and query keyed counts with std::map without relying on an absent key or accidental insertion during read-only work.

competencies.name: Persist line records with file streams
competencies.description: Read and write a documented text format through ifstream and ofstream using a stable project-relative path and complete record validation.

competencies.name: Preserve data across stream failures
competencies.description: Distinguish a missing first-run file, open failure, malformed content, normal end of file, and write failure before replacing existing data.

competencies.name: Debug one reproducible C++ failure
competencies.description: Build with warnings and debug symbols, reproduce one case, pause in VS Code or GDB, inspect relevant values and object state, repair one cause, and rerun the same case.

competencies.name: Verify behavior with dependency-free checks
competencies.description: Use small check functions to compare actual and expected normal, boundary, invalid, persistence, and no-mutation behavior with a visible summary.

competencies.name: Parse a small command-line contract
competencies.description: Validate argc before reading argv, parse bounded values, route supported commands, and show useful help for missing or unsupported input.

competencies.name: Document and publish a safe C++ repository
competencies.description: Write reproducible setup, compile, run, and check instructions; inspect staged paths; commit locally; and push source without binaries, credentials, private data, or editor caches.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A .cpp file stores source text; the compiler and linker produce a separate executable that Windows can run.
concepts.example: `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic banner.cpp -o banner.exe` builds before `.\banner.exe` runs.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming edited source is running merely because it is open in VS Code.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Each translation unit is compiled, then referenced definitions are connected during linking.
concepts.example: A declaration may compile while a missing definition produces an undefined-reference linker error.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling every build failure a syntax error.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Execution starts in main, whose returned integer reports success or failure to the surrounding process.
concepts.example: `return 0;` reports successful completion.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating printed text as the process exit status.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A warning or error gives a severity, source location, and message that should be read before editing.
concepts.example: A type-conversion warning identifies the source line and involved types.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing several lines before understanding the first relevant diagnostic.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A variable has a type, value, scope, and lifetime and should be initialized before its first read.
concepts.example: `int weekly_minutes{360};` creates an initialized integer.
concepts.commonMistake: Reading an uninitialized local variable.

concepts.simpleMeaning: The << operator sends values to an output stream in sequence; formatting state affects later numeric output.
concepts.example: `std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(1) << score;` controls decimal display.
concepts.commonMistake: Expecting commas inside a stream chain to behave like <<.

concepts.simpleMeaning: std::getline reads one complete line, including internal spaces, and reports whether extraction succeeded.
concepts.example: `std::getline(std::cin, name)` preserves a two-word name.
concepts.commonMistake: Mixing formatted extraction with getline and accidentally consuming a pending newline.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A numeric input is valid only when conversion succeeds, the whole intended text is consumed, and the value is in range.
concepts.example: `std::from_chars` can report both an error code and where parsing stopped.
concepts.commonMistake: Accepting `18cats` as the number 18.

concepts.simpleMeaning: std::string owns its text, tracks its size, and supports value comparison and concatenation.
concepts.example: `course == "CSC 101"` compares text contents.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating string storage like a manually terminated character buffer.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An if/else-if/else chain takes the first matching branch, so invalid cases belong before dependent success rules.
concepts.example: Reject an age outside the allowed range before testing eligibility.
concepts.commonMistake: Placing a broad success condition before a required rejection.

concepts.simpleMeaning: && and || evaluate left to right and may skip the right side when the result is already known.
concepts.example: `units > 0 && completed <= units` protects the second rule with the first.
concepts.commonMistake: Using a bitwise operator for a Boolean validation rule.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A loop needs deliberate initial state, a condition, and an update that can move the condition toward false.
concepts.example: A while loop removes one validated line from the input plan each iteration.
concepts.commonMistake: Updating the wrong value and creating an endless loop.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A vector owns a dynamic sequence indexed from zero through size minus one.
concepts.example: `scores.at(index)` checks the requested position.
concepts.commonMistake: Using index <= scores.size().

concepts.simpleMeaning: A range-based for visits each element when direct iterator or index control is unnecessary.
concepts.example: `for (const int score : scores)` reads every score.
concepts.commonMistake: Copying a large object in a read-only loop without noticing.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Some calculations need at least one value and must check emptiness before division, min, max, or dereference.
concepts.example: Return no summary until `scores.empty()` is false.
concepts.commonMistake: Dividing by size before checking for zero.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A function contract states parameter types, return type, responsibility, and relevant preconditions.
concepts.example: `double average(const std::vector<int>& values)` promises a calculated result without copying or mutation.
concepts.commonMistake: Combining input, calculation, storage, and printing in one function.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A value parameter is independent of its argument, and a value return gives the caller an owned result.
concepts.example: `Plan normalized(Plan input)` can return a separate adjusted value.
concepts.commonMistake: Returning a reference to a local variable.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A const reference lets a function observe an existing object without copying or permitting mutation through that name.
concepts.example: `const std::vector<int>& scores` provides read-only access.
concepts.commonMistake: Using a non-const reference for a function that should only inspect.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A header declares a shared interface; each .cpp file is compiled as its own translation unit before linking.
concepts.example: Both `main.cpp` and `planner.cpp` must be named in the g++ command.
concepts.commonMistake: Putting ordinary non-inline function definitions in a header and causing duplicate definitions.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A namespace groups related names and avoids placing course functions in the global namespace.
concepts.example: `campus::total_minutes(plan)` identifies its owner.
concepts.commonMistake: Writing `using namespace std;` in a header.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A constructor establishes an object state that member functions can safely assume is valid.
concepts.example: `Equipment{"Camera", 2}` begins with a nonblank label and nonnegative stock.
concepts.commonMistake: Constructing an invalid object and hoping later code repairs it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Private fields change only through controlled member functions; const member functions promise not to alter observable state.
concepts.example: `int available() const` reports stock without mutation.
concepts.commonMistake: Making fields public so callers can create negative stock.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Standard-library values own their resources and clean them up automatically; copying a value creates an independently managed value.
concepts.example: Copying an Equipment object and changing the copy does not change the original.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming two ordinary value objects secretly share the same fields.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Resource acquisition is tied to object lifetime, so local streams and containers release their resources when scope ends.
concepts.example: An ofstream closes when its owning object leaves scope, while explicit close can expose final write failure.
concepts.commonMistake: Using new/delete for a beginner record that std::vector and std::string already own safely.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Standard algorithms operate on a half-open range from a first iterator up to but not including a last iterator.
concepts.example: `std::sort(members.begin(), members.end(), predicate)` covers the whole vector.
concepts.commonMistake: Passing iterators from different containers.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A lambda states its parameters and which surrounding values it may use.
concepts.example: `[minimum](const Member& member) { return member.points >= minimum; }` captures one value.
concepts.commonMistake: Using `[&]` broadly and hiding which state controls the predicate.

concepts.simpleMeaning: std::map stores unique keys in ordered lookup form and can summarize counts by category.
concepts.example: `counts[course] += 1` intentionally inserts or increments a course count.
concepts.commonMistake: Using operator[] for a read-only lookup and accidentally inserting a missing key.

concepts.simpleMeaning: ifstream reads and ofstream writes; opening an output file normally replaces its contents unless a safer replacement plan is used.
concepts.example: `std::ifstream input{path};` never truncates the file.
concepts.commonMistake: Opening the live data path for output before validating all existing records.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A persisted line is valid only when every required field, delimiter, and range is accepted.
concepts.example: `id|topic|minutes` requires three complete fields and allowed values.
concepts.commonMistake: Loading a partial record and silently inventing the missing field.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A missing first-run file may mean empty state, while an existing malformed or unreadable file must stop without replacement.
concepts.example: A confirmed absent tracker file starts empty; a bad line preserves the original file.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating every failed open as a harmless first run.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A breakpoint pauses one reproducible case so actual variables, container contents, and object state can be inspected before repair.
concepts.example: Pause before choosing next_id and inspect highest_id and candidate.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding random print statements and editing multiple causes at once.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A small dependency-free check compares an actual result with a fixed expected contract and reports a visible pass or failure.
concepts.example: `check_equal("next id", 4, actual)` protects a named rule.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing the expected result merely to make a broken implementation pass.

concepts.simpleMeaning: argc counts command-line tokens and argv stores their text; count must be validated before indexing.
concepts.example: `coursepilot.exe add "CSC 101" "Revise vectors"` supplies a command and two values.
concepts.commonMistake: Reading argv[2] before confirming it exists.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A repository is reviewable when source, checks, safe samples, and README reproduce the build without generated or private files.
concepts.example: README records the exact C++20 build, run, and check commands.
concepts.commonMistake: Publishing .exe files, object files, secrets, personal records, or machine-specific editor paths.

resources.title: Install MSYS2 in its supported Windows location

location.start: Begin at MSYS2 Installer and read the GUI installer description plus installation-folder recommendations.
location.stop: Stop when the MSYS2 terminal opens; do not change mirrors, choose a spaced/non-ASCII path, install arbitrary packages, or disable Windows security controls.
location.note:
Do: Download the current x86_64 GUI installer from the official destination, install to `C:\msys64`, launch once, and record the installed version. Use the checksum guidance if download integrity is uncertain.

Finished when: MSYS2 opens from its supported short Windows path and is ready for the UCRT64 toolchain.

resources.title: Use the GCC warning contract as evidence

location.stop: Stop after the clean C++20 rebuild; do not add `-Werror`, analyzers, optimizers, sanitizers, or target-specific switches.

resources.title: Initialize and update values deliberately

location.stop: Stop before initialization edge cases, attributes, multiple declarations on one line, and chapter quiz material not used by the banner.

resources.title: Choose a fitting type for each banner value

resources.title: Read complete console lines into std::string

location.start: Begin at Introduction to std::string and continue through Use std::getline() to input text.
location.stop: Stop before string_view, advanced capacity details, and chapter exercises unrelated to line input.
location.note:
Do: Enter `Ada Lovelace` first with `operator>>` and then with `std::getline`; record what remained in the stream and keep the complete line in a `std::string`. Then include `<cctype>` and write this exact beginner helper: `bool has_non_whitespace(const std::string& text) { for (const unsigned char ch : text) { if (!std::isspace(ch)) return true; } return false; }`. Verify that an empty string and three spaces return false while `Mary Ann` returns true.

Finished when: The learner can explain why token extraction loses spaces, capture a complete line, and distinguish whitespace-only text from a usable name without deleting the learner's original spacing.

Next: Confirm the exact getline stream-state contract in the library reference.

resources.whySelected: The maintained lesson starts from beginner string use and explicitly contrasts token extraction with `std::getline` for names and other input containing spaces.

resources.title: Inspect the std::getline success contract

location.start: Read the overload summary, Behavior, and Return value for `std::getline` with `std::string`.
location.stop: Stop before allocator overload details, wide-character examples, and defect-report history.
location.note:
Do: Trace three fixtures: `Ada Lovelace`, an empty line, and end-of-input. Record the stored string and stream state, then write `if (!std::getline(std::cin, line))` before inspecting the line.

Finished when: The learner distinguishes a successfully read blank line from a read that never produced a line.

Next: Parse a complete numeric line without accepting trailing junk.

resources.whySelected: The canonical cppreference URL defines delimiter extraction and fail/eof behavior precisely enough to distinguish a blank line from a failed read.

resources.title: Validate a full numeric line with std::istringstream

location.start: Read the class summary, the `std::istringstream` alias, constructor link, and inherited `operator>>`/stream-state entries only.
location.stop: Stop before custom stream buffers, move/swap, `rdbuf`, locales, exception masks, and writing a parser from scratch.
location.note:
Do: Use this exact helper body after including `<sstream>`: `std::istringstream input{text}; int candidate{}; if (!(input >> candidate)) return false; input >> std::ws; if (!input.eof()) return false; result = candidate; return true;`. Run it against `42`, ` 42 `, `42x`, `42 7`, an empty line, and `101` with a later 15..100 range check.

Finished when: The learner rejects partial conversions and keeps the destination unchanged whenever the complete line is invalid.

Next: Order range and category rules so only one decision wins.

resources.whySelected: The C++ library reference establishes that `std::istringstream` performs normal input operations over a string, matching the supplied beginner parsing helper without introducing third-party code.

resources.title: Make ordered decisions and boundaries explicit

location.start: Read Quick if-statement recap, If or else with multiple conditional statements, and If-else vs if-if.
location.stop: Stop before constexpr-if and advanced conditional forms; do not use nested ternaries or switch for range rules.
location.note:
Do: Write expected results for ages 14, 15, 16, 100, and 101; then for CSC 102 prerequisite counts 0 and 1. Apply INVALID before NOT ELIGIBLE, PENDING PAYMENT, and ELIGIBLE in one braced chain; reverse two branches once and observe the wrong first match.

Finished when: The learner explains why branch order is part of behavior and proves each boundary with an expected-versus-actual record.

Next: Combine comparisons safely with logical operators and short-circuit evaluation.

resources.whySelected: The beginner lesson directly contrasts if/else-if with independent if statements and demonstrates why braces protect multi-statement decisions.

resources.title: Combine conditions and guard unsafe work

location.start: Read Logical NOT, Logical OR, Logical AND, and Short circuit evaluation.
location.stop: Stop before mixing long AND/OR chains, De Morgan transformations, bitwise operators, overloaded operators, and alternate operator keywords.
location.note:
Do: Trace these score/attendance rows against the rule score >= 50 AND attendance >= 75: 49/74, 50/74, 49/75, and 50/75. Compare AND with OR at each boundary, then evaluate `count != 0 && total / count >= 50` for zero and nonzero count before running it locally.

Finished when: The learner chooses AND versus OR from the written rule and explains why a false left operand prevents the guarded division from running.

Next: Take the Week 2 Skill Check, then build the Enrollment Eligibility Assistant.

resources.whySelected: The maintained beginner lesson teaches `!`, `&&`, `||`, their truth behavior, and the left-to-right short-circuit rule used by this week’s validation decisions.

location.start: Begin at Introduction to std::vector and read through Accessing array elements and Subscript out of bounds.

location.note:
Do: Create an empty `std::vector<int>`, a list-initialized vector, and `std::vector<int> scores{45, 60, 75}`. Draw the valid indices for the non-empty vectors, read known valid elements with `operator[]`, and predict why index `size()` is outside the range.

Finished when: The learner can create and inspect an owned vector and states that a non-empty vector’s last valid index is one less than its size.

Next: Use the container reference to grow the vector and compare checked versus unchecked access.

resources.whySelected: The maintained lesson introduces vector element type, list construction, zero-based indexing, and out-of-bounds risk without detouring through raw arrays or manual allocation.

resources.title: Grow a vector and use checked access deliberately

location.start: Read the vector summary, then open only Element access for `at`/`operator[]`, Capacity for `empty`/`size`, and Modifiers for `push_back`.
location.stop: Stop before allocators, capacity tuning, iterator invalidation detail, insertion/erasure variants, `vector<bool>`, ranges additions, and exception internals.
location.note:
Do: Start with an empty `std::vector<int>`, append 20 and 45 with `push_back`, and record size after each step. Predict the valid range, run `values.at(2)` once to observe the checked out-of-range failure, then remove that failing call and guard ordinary access with `index < values.size()`.

Finished when: The learner can append one validated value, report the new size, use `at` for the checked demonstration, and guard ordinary indexing with `i < size()`.

Next: Traverse the vector without indexing when only element values are needed.

resources.whySelected: The vector reference lists `push_back`, `at`, `operator[]`, `size`, and `empty` together, making it a bounded lookup surface for operations the learner immediately runs on explicit fixtures.

resources.title: Traverse vectors with range-for and const references

location.start: Read Range-based for loops, Empty containers, and Avoid element copies using references.
location.stop: Stop before custom range types, proxy references, and advanced iterator mechanics; never add or erase elements inside this traversal.
location.note:
Do: Use `std::vector<int> scores{45, 60, 75}`. Print with `const auto&`, sum with a value element, then add 5 to the value copy and prove the vector is unchanged. Repeat with `auto&` only to clamp a disposable copy of `{20, 120}` to a maximum of 100.

Finished when: The learner distinguishes an element copy, modifiable reference, and read-only reference and picks the least-permissive form.

Next: Compute count, total, minimum, and maximum safely, including the empty case.

resources.whySelected: The lesson makes range-for behavior, empty containers, copies, `auto&`, and `const auto&` explicit and recommends safer traversal when indices are unnecessary.

resources.title: Summarize a collection without inventing empty data

location.start: Read the library overview, then find `min_element` and `max_element` in Minimum/maximum operations.
location.stop: Stop before execution policies, ranges views, heaps, permutations, parallelism, and algorithms not used by the Week 3 build.
location.note:
Do: For `{}`, `{45}`, and `{20, 45, 30, 60}`, predict whether a min/max iterator may be dereferenced. Guard empty first, calculate count and total, then compare local results with the two named algorithms.

Finished when: The learner reports honest summaries for empty and non-empty vectors and never dereferences an end iterator.

Next: Take the Week 3 Skill Check, then build the Study Session Analyzer.

resources.whySelected: The canonical algorithms index groups non-modifying queries, min/max, and numeric operations and makes iterator/range boundaries visible.

resources.title: Visual route: give one function one clear job

location.start: Start at 02:03:10, Functions.
location.stop: Stop at 02:16:42 when Function overloading begins; do not use overloading, templates, global variables, or hidden input inside calculation functions.
location.note:

Finished when: The learner can declare, define, call, and test a small value-returning function whose contract fits in one sentence.

Next: Choose whether each parameter should be copied or observed through a const reference.

resources.whySelected: The free chapter demonstrates declarations, parameters, arguments, calls, and return values in a short runnable sequence before its later overloading material.

resources.title: Pass small values by value and larger read-only inputs by const reference

location.start: Read Pass by const reference, Const references can accept modifiable lvalues, const lvalues, and rvalues, and When to pass by const reference.
location.stop: Stop before move semantics, forwarding references, reference collapsing, lifetime-extension edge cases, and micro-benchmarking.
location.note:
Do: Implement `int total_credits(const std::vector<int>& values)` with a range-for sum, call it using named data and a temporary vector, then attempt one mutation inside it and read the compiler diagnostic. Keep `int remaining_credits(int target, int completed)` by value and explain both choices.

Finished when: The learner can justify value versus `const&` from mutation intent and ordinary copy cost, not habit.

Next: Move a working function into a second source file without losing its declaration.

resources.whySelected: The maintained lesson directly explains copy cost, const safety, literals, and the practical difference between value and const-reference parameters without requiring ownership tricks.

resources.title: Compile a program from more than one source file

location.start: Read Adding files to your project, A multi-file example, and the compiler-command note for command-line users.
location.stop: Stop before separate compilation scripts, libraries, build systems, unity builds, modules, and CMake.
location.note:
Do: Begin with `int credits_remaining(int target, int completed) { return target - completed; }` in `main.cpp`. Move that definition into `planner.cpp`, leave its declaration temporarily in `main.cpp`, and compile both files together. Then omit `planner.cpp` once, capture the linker error, and repair the command.

Finished when: The learner can distinguish a compiler error from a linker error and build `main.cpp` plus `planner.cpp` in one command.

Next: Replace the temporary declaration with a guarded header and keep names out of the global namespace.

resources.whySelected: The lesson shows the exact declaration, definition, linker, and compile-command relationship needed for a small multi-file beginner project.

resources.title: Declare the planner interface once in a guarded header

location.start: Read Duplicate definitions and a compile error, Header guards, and Updating our previous example with header guards.
location.stop: Stop before precompiled headers, modules, transitive-include debates, macros beyond a header guard, and `using namespace` directives in headers.
location.note:
Do: Create a guarded `planner.hpp`, move `int total_credits(const std::vector<int>&);` and `int total_minutes(const std::vector<int>&);` into it, include it from `main.cpp` and `planner.cpp`, then compile with `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.cpp planner.cpp -o module-planner.exe`. Include the header twice in a disposable check to confirm the guard.

Finished when: The learner can explain which file owns each declaration and definition and can rebuild after changing either source file.

Next: Place the planner interface in one named namespace and call it with an explicit qualified name.

resources.whySelected: The focused lesson shows the duplicate-inclusion problem, a complete guard, and why declarations belong in guarded headers without forcing a new build system.

resources.title: Group the planner interface in a named namespace

location.start: Read Defining your own namespaces and Accessing a namespace with the scope resolution operator.
location.stop: Stop before nested, unnamed, inline, aliased, versioned, and multi-level organizational namespaces; do not add `using namespace` to a header.
location.note:
Do: Wrap the planner declarations and matching definitions in `namespace campus { ... }`, call `campus::total_credits(...)` from main, then create a disposable global function with the same short name to prove the qualified call remains unambiguous.

Finished when: The learner writes one named namespace, keeps declarations and definitions aligned inside it, and calls a member with `campus::` explicitly.

Next: Take the Week 4 Skill Check, then build the Module Planner Library.

resources.whySelected: The focused beginner lesson shows the exact `namespace Name {}` definition and `Name::member` call syntax used by the multi-file planner.

resources.title: Visual route: model an equipment loan as an object

location.start: Start at 05:18:38, Object Oriented Programming.
location.stop: Stop at 05:48:59 before Inheritance; do not add inheritance, virtual methods, raw pointers, or a framework.
location.note:
Do: Watch classes/objects, constructors, constructor overloading, and getters/setters. Recreate only one simple class, list the state that must be valid after construction, and predict which attempted invalid update its method should reject.

Finished when: The learner can construct two independent objects and explain how a public operation preserves one class rule.

Next: Refine that first class with private state and small public behavior.

resources.whySelected: This bounded beginner chapter makes class members, construction, and controlled state visible in runnable examples without introducing inheritance into the assignment.

resources.title: Keep class state private and behavior small

location.start: Read Member access, Access specifiers, and Access level best practices for structs and classes.
location.stop: Stop before per-class access nuances, friends, protected access, inheritance, and advanced encapsulation design.
location.note:
Do: Classify `label_`, `total_`, and `available_` as private state; classify `label()`, `total()`, `available()`, `status_line()`, `borrow_one()`, and `return_one()` as public observations/actions. Confirm a caller cannot assign an invalid count directly while each operation can reject an impossible transition.

Finished when: The learner can explain why private state plus a narrow public operation makes an invalid transition harder to express.

Next: Use a constructor and member initializer list to make every new loan valid immediately.

resources.whySelected: The focused lesson explains public versus private access and recommends private data with public member behavior, directly supporting the invariant boundary introduced by the visual class lesson.

resources.title: Establish valid state with a constructor initializer list

location.start: Read Member initializer lists and Member initialization order only.
location.stop: Stop before delegating constructors, converting constructors, copy/move constructors, exceptions-as-policy, and dynamic allocation.
location.note:
Do: Start from this exact standalone shape inside `namespace campus`: `Equipment::Equipment(std::string label, int total) : label_{label}, total_{total}, available_{total} {}`. Compile it with the previously declared `label_`, `total_`, and `available_` fields; construct `Equipment{"Camera", 2}` and `Equipment{"Projector", 1}`. Reorder the written initializer list once, inspect the reorder warning, then restore declaration order and rebuild cleanly. The Week 5 Build later adds the bounded validation body.

Finished when: Every successfully created object satisfies the stated required-field rule, and initialization order follows member declaration order.

Next: Add one tightly bounded throw/try/catch path for invalid construction and invalid state transitions.

resources.whySelected: The focused lesson shows direct member initialization and initialization order, letting learners establish invariants without setter-first or partially initialized objects.

resources.title: Report bounded class failures with throw, try, and catch

location.start: Read Throwing exceptions, Looking for exceptions, Handling exceptions, and Putting throw, try, and catch together.
location.stop: Stop before stack unwinding detail, catch-all handlers, custom exception classes, exception specifications, rethrowing, nested exceptions, and exception-safety taxonomy.
location.note:
Do: Include `<cctype>` and `<stdexcept>`. Write `bool has_non_whitespace(const std::string& text) { for (const unsigned char ch : text) { if (!std::isspace(ch)) return true; } return false; }`. Trace `if (!has_non_whitespace(label)) throw std::invalid_argument{"label must not be blank"};` inside construction, then run that construction inside `try` and catch `const std::invalid_argument& error`. Repeat with `throw std::logic_error{"no item is available"};` before a borrow mutation, and record state before and after.

Finished when: The learner can identify the throw point and matching handler and can show that each rejected request occurs before any class member changes.

Next: Let standard value members own their own lifetime instead of managing memory manually.

resources.whySelected: This focused lesson introduces the three C++ mechanisms the supplied class scaffold uses to reject construction or transition requests without returning a half-valid object.

resources.title: Use value ownership and RAII; do not write new or delete

location.start: Read the RAII summary, the lifetime guarantee bullets, and the Standard Library examples naming `std::string`, `std::vector`, and smart ownership.
location.stop: Stop before mutex examples, custom resource wrappers, exception guarantees, smart-pointer graphs, move internals, and allocator details.
location.note:
Do: Trace when a local item and a local `std::vector<Equipment>` are constructed and destroyed as a function enters and leaves scope. Run `items.push_back(camera); Equipment practice_copy{camera}; items.pop_back();` and confirm that no cleanup function, `new`, `delete`, owning raw pointer, or manual array is needed.

Finished when: The learner can describe who owns each string and loan value and why normal scope exit performs the required cleanup.

Next: Take the Week 5 Skill Check, then build the Equipment Loan Desk.

resources.whySelected: The canonical language reference connects object lifetime, scope, and standard containers to automatic resource cleanup while explicitly naming RAII-enabled library types.

resources.title: Read iterator pairs as a half-open sequence

location.start: Read Introduction to iterators, The end marker, and Iterator invalidation only.
location.stop: Stop before iterator categories, reverse/custom iterators, ranges, pointer equivalence details, and writing iterator classes.
location.note:
Do: Draw `std::vector<int> values{10, 20, 30, 40}` and mark `begin()` and the one-past-end marker. Trace `for (auto it = values.begin(); it != values.end(); ++it)`, state why `end()` cannot be dereferenced, then invalidate an iterator with `push_back(50)` and reacquire it before reuse.

Finished when: The learner can trace a half-open iterator range and avoids dereferencing end or reusing a knowingly invalidated iterator.

Next: Use that range with named library algorithms instead of rewriting their loops.

resources.whySelected: The lesson introduces begin/end, dereference, increment, and invalidation as the vocabulary used by standard algorithms, without requiring learners to implement an iterator.

resources.title: Find, count, and sort with named standard algorithms

location.start: Read Finding elements with std::find, Finding elements with std::find_if, Using std::count and std::count_if, and Sorting with std::sort.
location.stop: Stop before ranges algorithms, execution policies, custom iterator types, and algorithm chains not needed by the roster.
location.note:
Do: Use the Week 6 roster values `104/Amina/CSC/80`, `101/Tola/EEE/65`, `109/Kofi/CSC/80`, `103/Lami/MAT/45`, and `107/Uche/EEE/70`. Predict found, missing, and empty searches; use `find_if` for ID 107 and check `end()` before access; use `count_if` for points >= 80; then sort a copied roster and prove original order is unchanged.

Finished when: The learner selects `find_if`, `count_if`, or `sort` from the intended result, handles not-found safely, and states whether each call observes or changes its range.

Next: Supply one narrow custom rule with an explicitly captured lambda.

resources.whySelected: The maintained beginner lesson gives runnable `std::find_if`, `std::count_if`, and `std::sort` examples and shows the not-found check required before iterator dereference.

resources.title: Visual route: write a small explicit-capture lambda

location.start: Start at 17:20:25, Capture Lists. Use `[targetId](const Member& member) { return member.id() == targetId; }` and `[minimum](const Member& member) { return member.points() >= minimum; }` as the two bounded syntax models.
location.stop: Stop when Capture All begins or at 17:40:08, whichever comes first; skip default capture practice, mutable lambdas, generic lambdas, and unrelated chapter material.
location.note:
Do: Watch the capture-list explanation and first explicit capture-by-value example. Label capture, parameter, body, and return in the ID predicate, run it for ID 107, then adapt the same shape to `minimum = 80`. Change the outer value after each lambda is created and predict whether its stored capture changes.

Finished when: The learner can write and explain a short predicate with a named capture and refuses `[&]` or `[=]` when one explicit name is sufficient.

Next: Aggregate roster membership by course code under stable string keys with std::map.

resources.whySelected: The C++20 course has a dedicated lambda chapter with named capture-list examples; the tight assignment excludes generic and advanced lambda material.

resources.title: Build keyed summaries with std::map

location.start: Read the first summary paragraphs, Iterator invalidation, and the entries for `at`, `find`, `contains`, and `operator[]` only.
location.stop: Stop before allocators, node handles, heterogeneous lookup, deduction guides, merge internals, custom comparators, and performance proofs.
location.note:
Do: Start with `std::map<std::string, int> counts{{"CSC", 1}}`. Predict empty, new-key, repeat-key, and missing-key results; run `++counts["EEE"]` and `++counts["CSC"]`; read CSC with `at`; then check ART with `find` or `contains` before access and prove map size did not change.

Finished when: The learner produces correct per-course counts and distinguishes inserting access from checked lookup.

Next: Transform display names into a separate output range without mutating stored records.

resources.whySelected: The canonical container page states map uniqueness, sorted keys, lookup behavior, and member operations in one stable reference used for a narrowly scaffolded exercise.

resources.title: Transform values into a separate output range

location.start: Read the first unary overload, Parameters, Return value, and only the unary uppercase portion of the example.
location.stop: Stop before binary transform, execution policies, ranges overloads, in-place mutation, implementation code, and locale-specific conversion.
location.note:
Do: Pre-size a destination `std::vector<std::string>` to the source size. Use this supplied character step inside an `uppercase_copy` helper: `ch = static_cast<char>(std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(ch)));`. Transform Amina and Tola into the destination, include `<cctype>`, and compare stored names before and after.

Finished when: The learner identifies the input range and destination, produces one display value per source member, and proves the stored roster names remain unchanged.

Next: Check the strict comparator rule required by std::sort before the Skill Check.

resources.whySelected: The focused algorithm reference states the source range, destination start, unary operation, and returned output iterator needed by the roster’s non-mutating display conversion.

resources.title: Make a sort comparator strict and deterministic

location.start: Read the Compare summary and only the strict weak ordering bullets for `comp(a, a)`, opposite directions, and transitivity.
location.stop: Stop before equivalence-class proofs, container requirement tables, concepts, mathematical notation beyond the three listed properties, and custom comparator types.
location.note:
Do: Evaluate both `left.points() >= right.points()` and `left.points() > right.points()` when left and right are the same 80-point record. Then write the complete rule: higher points first; when points match, lower name first. Trace Amina/80 against Kofi/80 in both directions.

Finished when: The learner explains why `>=` is invalid for equal elements and produces a deterministic points-descending, name-ascending comparator that is false for self-comparison.

Next: Take the Week 6 Skill Check, then build the Campus Club Roster.

resources.whySelected: The canonical Compare requirement states the exact self-comparison and direction rules that distinguish a valid strict comparator from the tempting `>=` defect in the roster.

resources.title: Read and write simple line records with file streams

location.start: Read File output using ofstream, File input using ifstream, and File modes only.
location.stop: Stop before binary I/O, random access, stream buffering internals, serialization libraries, and platform-specific file APIs.
location.note:
Do: Write `1|Loops|45` and `2|Vectors|60` to a temporary file, close by leaving scope, reopen it, and read each full line with `std::getline`. Compare the reloaded lines with the originals and inspect the file in the editor.

Finished when: The learner can save and reload complete line records and checks stream state before treating a file operation as successful.

Next: Make failed reads and malformed records preserve the last valid in-memory state.

resources.whySelected: The beginner lesson covers file stream headers, open modes, line input, stream state, and automatic close behavior with standard-library types only.

resources.title: Preserve valid state when a file cannot be trusted

location.start: Read the class summary and only the File operations and State functions tables: `open`, `is_open`, `close`, `good`, `fail`, and `bad`.
location.stop: Stop before stream buffers, locales, callbacks, exceptions masks, binary modes, and opening an output stream before input validation succeeds.
location.note:
Do: Run five exact fixtures: absent `missing.txt`; directory path `not-a-regular-file`; empty `empty.txt`; valid lines `1|Loops|45` and `2|Vectors|60`; and malformed line `2|Vectors`. Begin live memory with one sentinel record, parse into a temporary vector, and replace the sentinel only after the whole valid file succeeds.

Finished when: A failed or malformed load reports a useful error and leaves the previously valid tracker state unchanged.

Next: Use the debugger to locate the exact branch or value that violates this contract.

resources.whySelected: The canonical `basic_fstream` page exposes open, is_open, state checks, and close operations needed to reason about failure without inventing a custom file abstraction.

resources.title: Inspect one record-validation value with GDB in VS Code

location.start: Open only Debug helloworld.cpp; in that walkthrough read Step through the code, Set a watch, and Customize debugging with launch.json.
location.stop: Stop after the repaired fixture passes; skip IntelliSense customization, remote debugging, disassembly, conditional function breakpoints, and Visual Studio-only tooling.
location.note:
Do: Create a throwaway `debug-fixture.cpp` using the already learned headers and this exact body: `std::string record{"2|Vectors"}; int separators{}; for (const char ch : record) if (ch == '|') ++separators; const bool valid{separators == 2}; std::cout << valid << "\n";`. Compile with `-g`, break on the `std::cout` line after `valid` has been initialized, and inspect `record`, `separators`, and `valid` in Variables or Watch. Record the malformed result, change only the fixture to `2|Vectors|45`, and rerun the same breakpoint. The later Build supplies its own tracker-specific launch configuration.

Finished when: The learner records the exact fixture, breakpoint, observed separator count, expected validity, one focused repair, and the rerun result without needing the locked Build scaffold.

Next: Keep that behavior protected with a tiny dependency-free check harness.

resources.whySelected: The official guide matches the installed editor and GDB toolchain and demonstrates breakpoints, stepping, variable inspection, and debug configuration without another service.

resources.title: Translate a testing idea into plain C++ checks

location.start: Read the README introduction and its first `TEST_CASE`/`REQUIRE` example only.
location.stop: Stop before installation, CMake integration, generators, matchers, sections, benchmarks, or adopting the framework in this course.
location.note:
Do: Identify the test name, action, and independent expected result in the example. Do not clone or install Catch2. In a throwaway file, define `int checks_run{}; int failures{};` and a `check_true(label, condition)` function that increments checks_run, prints PASS or FAIL with the label, and increments failures only on false. Use it for the five earlier Study outcomes (missing, non-regular, empty, valid, malformed), print `(checks_run - failures)/checks_run`, and return nonzero when failures is not zero. The later Build supplies the generic `check_equal` variant.

Finished when: The learner can rerun a clearly named plain-C++ check set, see expected versus actual on failure, and rely on its exit status.

Next: Plan the exact candidate, backup, promotion, and rollback states before the Build supplies its filesystem helper.

resources.whySelected: The mature open-source project README provides a credible compact example of named test cases and expected results; the course deliberately borrows the idea, not the dependency.

resources.title: Plan a failure-preserving candidate and backup sequence

location.start: Read the filesystem summary, then open only `exists`, `rename`, and `remove`; inspect the overloads that receive `std::error_code&`.
location.stop: Stop before directory iteration, permissions, links, canonical paths, recursive removal, timestamps, exceptions, race-condition design, and implementing a generic storage library.
location.note:
Do: In `replacement-trace.md`, trace this supplied sequence without writing filesystem code: validate and fully close `.tmp`; refuse a pre-existing `.bak`; when live exists rename live to `.bak`; rename `.tmp` to live; on failed promotion rename `.bak` back to live and report failure; only after successful promotion remove `.bak`, treating cleanup failure as a warning. Complete three tables: no live file, successful replacement, and failed promotion with rollback. At every row record which of live/tmp/bak exists and which bytes remain authoritative.

Finished when: The learner can explain the candidate/backup state machine and why success is reported only after promotion, before the unlocked Build provides the actual helper implementation.

Next: Take the Week 7 Skill Check, then build the Persistent Revision Tracker.

resources.whySelected: The canonical filesystem index links the exact C++17 operations used by the visible helper scaffold and documents their error-reporting boundary without requiring platform-specific Windows calls.

resources.title: Accept an exact CoursePilot command through main arguments

location.stop: Stop before environment pointers, implementation-specific signatures, Unicode command-line APIs, parsing libraries, shell scripting, and subcommand frameworks.

Label every argv element, reject both missing and extra arguments before access, and return success/failure deliberately. Add a `may write?` column: only a fully validated successful `add` or `complete` may reach saving; a missing ID, repeated completion, unknown command, bad argument count, `list`, `summary`, or `help` must not write storage.

Finished when: The learner never reads a missing argument and can run every supported command from the terminal with an intentional exit status.

Next: Integrate the earlier class, collection, algorithm, file, and check contracts behind those commands.

resources.whySelected: The canonical language page defines the portable `argc`/`argv` forms, argument count, program name, and return status without a command-line framework.

resources.title: Plan a source-only GitHub handoff

location.stop: Stop after the written plan and fictional classification; do not publish before the CoursePilot Build, pre-push safety review, and local checks are complete, and never force-push, rewrite shared history, or paste access tokens into commands or files.

resources.title: Write a reproducible CoursePilot README

`g++ -std=c++20 src\profile.cpp -o out\profile.exe`
`g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic src\profile.cpp -o out\profile.exe`
`g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic out\profile.exe -o src\profile.cpp`

questions.explanation: `g++` selects the C++ driver, `-std=c++20` fixes the language version, the warning flags expose suspicious code, and `-o` names the executable.

questions.prompt: Which signature names the standard no-argument entry point for this week’s C++ console program?

`long main()`
`int main;`
`int main()`

questions.explanation: `int main()` is the standard entry-point signature; its function body supplies the statements and return status. The other forms do not declare C++’s required entry function.

questions.prompt: Given `std::string name = "Ada";` and `int level = 1;`, which statement prints `Ada | 1` followed by a newline?

options.label: `std::cout << name, " | ", level, "\n";`
`std::cout << name << " | " << level << "\n";`
`std::cout >> name >> " | " >> level;`
`std::cin << name << " | " << level << "\n";`

questions.explanation: The `<<` operators insert each value into `std::cout` in sequence. `std::cin` reads input, and the other forms are not this course’s valid stream syntax.

questions.prompt: What does `int attempts{1}; attempts = attempts + 1;` leave in `attempts`?

options.label: A string containing `11`

questions.explanation: Brace initialization creates an integer with value 1. The later arithmetic expression produces 2 and assignment stores that value back.

questions.prompt: Why is `int sessions{2.5};` rejected by a conforming C++ compiler?

options.label: The compiler rounds `2.5` first, and brace syntax rejects every rounded result
The decimal literal changes the declared variable itself from `int` to `double`
Brace initialization prevents this narrowing conversion from `double` to `int`
The value is accepted as `2`, but braces require an unused-value warning

questions.explanation: List initialization diagnoses a conversion that would discard the fractional part. That protection makes the loss visible instead of silently accepting it.

questions.prompt: A missing closing quote triggers several compiler messages on later lines. What is the strongest first move?

options.label: Repair the earliest useful diagnostic, rebuild with the same command, then reassess later messages
Repair the last diagnostic first because it is closest to the end of the file
Edit every line named by a diagnostic before rebuilding the program once
Suppress the first diagnostic and treat the remaining messages as independent causes

questions.explanation: One malformed token can confuse parsing of everything that follows. Repairing the earliest useful cause and rebuilding produces cleaner evidence.

questions.prompt: You change a displayed name in `profile.cpp`, but running `profile.exe` still shows the old name. The run path is correct. What should you check first?

options.label: Whether the terminal still displays buffered text even after a successful rebuild
Whether the source was saved and the executable was rebuilt successfully
Whether rebuilding a different source file in the same folder should update this executable
Whether rerunning the old executable can compile the edited source automatically

questions.explanation: An existing executable does not reread edited source. Saving and rebuilding must replace it before the new behavior can appear.

questions.prompt: The warning-enabled build finishes and creates the executable. What has that result established?

options.label: Every required value and layout is correct
The program has passed every future input case
This source compiled and linked; its runtime behavior still needs checking
The repository is already safe to publish

questions.explanation: Compilation establishes that the translation and link steps succeeded. It does not prove that runtime output satisfies the learner’s contract.

questions.prompt: The compiler reports an unused variable named `score`. What response best supports a warning-clean beginner program?

options.label: Decide whether `score` is required, then use it meaningfully or remove it before rebuilding
Print `score` in an extra debug line solely to silence the warning, even when the output contract does not need it
Rename it to `unusedScore` while leaving it unused, assuming the new name suppresses the compiler warning
Move the declaration to a wider scope without giving the value a purpose in the program

questions.explanation: The warning identifies a mismatch between declared intent and actual behavior. Using the value for its purpose or removing dead code resolves that mismatch directly.

skillCheck.title: Complete-Line Input, Strings, and Decisions Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: Which statement reads an entire line such as `Ada Lovelace` into `std::string name`?

options.label: `std::cin >> name;`
`std::getline(std::cin, name);`
`std::getline(name, std::cin);`
`std::cin.getline(name);`

questions.explanation: `std::getline` reads through the line delimiter, so embedded spaces remain part of the string. Formatted extraction with `>>` stops at whitespace.

questions.prompt: After `std::cin >> age;` successfully reads an integer, the next `std::getline(std::cin, name)` immediately returns an empty line. What is the likely cause?

options.label: The formatted extraction set end-of-file immediately after every valid integer
`getline` discards the first complete line whenever another extraction ran earlier
The destination string must be cleared manually before `getline` can replace it
The formatted extraction left the newline waiting in the input stream

questions.explanation: The numeric extraction consumes the number but normally leaves its delimiter. The next `getline` sees that pending newline as the end of an empty line.

questions.prompt: `std::getline(std::cin, line)` returns successfully and `line.empty()` is true. What has the program established?

options.label: A blank line was read successfully; whether blank input is allowed is a separate application rule
The read failed because a successful `getline` cannot produce an empty string
End-of-input occurred before extraction, and the empty string alone proves `failbit` is set
Every empty result should be discarded because it can only be a leftover delimiter

questions.explanation: `getline` can successfully extract a line containing no characters before its delimiter. The stream result establishes whether a line was read; the application then decides whether that blank value is valid.

questions.prompt: A learner is eligible only when `score >= 50` and `attendance >= 75`. Which condition states that rule?

options.label: `score >= 50 || attendance >= 75`
`score = 50 && attendance = 75`
`score >= 50 && attendance >= 75`
`score >= 50, attendance >= 75`

questions.explanation: Logical AND requires both comparisons to be true. OR would accept a learner who satisfies only one requirement, while assignment does not express comparison.

questions.prompt: Scores outside 0–100 are invalid. Which decision should run before pass/fail classification?

options.label: The invalid-range rejection
The fail branch
The pass branch
The final success message

questions.explanation: Invalid data is not an ordinary fail result. Rejecting its range first prevents later branches from assigning a misleading legitimate outcome.

questions.prompt: Why can `count != 0 && total / count >= 50` safely guard the division?

options.label: The right side is evaluated first so it can repair an invalid count
The comparison after the division converts a zero divisor into `false`
A false left side stops `&&` before the division
The guard works only because integer division returns zero when its divisor is zero

questions.explanation: Built-in `&&` short-circuits from left to right. A false guard decides the full expression, so the division is not attempted with zero.

questions.prompt: The supplied `istringstream` helper extracts an integer, consumes trailing whitespace, and requires end-of-stream. How should it classify the line `50points`?

options.label: Valid integer 50 because any numeric prefix is enough
Invalid because non-whitespace characters remain after the integer
Valid string that decisions compare numerically
End-of-file before any extraction

questions.explanation: Full-line validation requires both a successful integer extraction and no remaining non-whitespace input. Accepting only the prefix would misrepresent what the learner typed.

questions.prompt: The course helper reads with `std::istringstream`, extracts one integer, consumes whitespace, and requires no extra token. How should it treat `  75  `?

options.label: Invalid because the helper requires the first character to be a digit
Valid as 75 but only if the helper ignores all remaining characters without checking them
Invalid because trailing whitespace is treated as a second token
Valid as the integer 75

questions.explanation: Formatted integer extraction skips leading whitespace, and the explicit trailing-whitespace step permits spaces after the number while still rejecting extra content.

questions.prompt: Why does the course read numeric input into a `std::string` line first and then pass that line to the supplied parser?

options.label: It lets the parser accept a numeric prefix while safely ignoring any remaining suffix
It keeps line boundaries and lets the parser reject an invalid entry
It guarantees the parsed number is in range without a separate range check
It converts the line before any stream or parser failure needs to be inspected

questions.explanation: A line-first workflow avoids leftover-delimiter surprises and gives validation the complete text the learner submitted, including any invalid suffix.

questions.prompt: Which set most credibly checks both numeric parsing and an eligibility threshold of 50?

options.label: `50`, `49`, and invalid `50points` with no eligibility result
`49`, `50`, and `51`, all valid numeric lines
`50points`, a blank line, and `points50`, with no valid boundary value
`50` and invalid `50points`, but no value below the eligibility boundary

questions.explanation: The set checks the exact decision boundary, one value below it, and rejection of a tempting partial parse before any outcome is assigned.

skillCheck.title: Loops, Vectors, and Safe Summaries Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: Given `std::vector<int> minutes;` and a validated `int value`, which statement appends that value as a new final element?

options.label: `minutes.resize(value);`
`minutes.insert(minutes.begin(), value);`
`minutes.at(minutes.size()) = value;`
`minutes.push_back(value);`

questions.explanation: `push_back` grows the vector by one element and copies the validated value into the new final position.

questions.prompt: Before calculating `total / sessions.size()`, which condition identifies the case that must be handled separately?

options.label: `sessions.size() > total`
`sessions.empty()`
`sessions.front() == 0`
`total != 0`

questions.explanation: An empty vector has zero elements, so its size cannot be a divisor. A first element of zero is valid data and does not imply that no sessions exist.

questions.prompt: Which loop adds every integer in `sessions` to `total` without requiring an index?

options.label: `for (int value : sessions) { ++total; }`
`for (int value : sessions) { total = value; }`
`for (int value : sessions) { total += value; }`
`for (int value : total) { sessions += value; }`

questions.explanation: A range-based `for` visits each element. The loop variable receives each integer value, which can then be accumulated into `total`.

questions.prompt: Why does `for (int value : scores) { value += 5; }` leave the vector unchanged?

options.label: `value` is a copy of each element, so only the copy changes
The range-for loop restores every vector element from its original value after each iteration
`value` is an implicit const reference, so the assignment is accepted but discarded
The addition changes the vector capacity rather than the stored element values

questions.explanation: A plain `int` loop variable receives a copy. Mutating stored elements would require a non-const reference such as `int&`, if mutation were actually intended.

questions.prompt: A prompt should allow exactly three attempts unless valid input arrives earlier. Which control plan states that bound most clearly?

options.label: Reset the attempt counter after every invalid entry so each new entry receives three tries
Increment before each prompt and continue while a zero-based counter is less than or equal to three
Increment an attempt counter after each failed try and continue while it is below three
Use an unbounded loop and rely on the learner eventually entering a valid value

questions.explanation: A monotonic counter and explicit upper bound make termination inspectable. A successful-input branch can still leave the loop early.

questions.prompt: The vector is known to be non-empty and may contain negative values. What is a sound manual maximum strategy?

options.label: Start from the first element, then compare the remaining elements
Initialize the maximum to 0 and replace it only when an element is greater
Initialize the maximum to the vector size and compare every stored value with that count
Start from the final element but stop the comparison loop before visiting the first element

questions.explanation: Initializing from actual data avoids an invented zero that would incorrectly beat every negative element. The precondition that the vector is non-empty makes the first element available.

questions.prompt: For sessions `{20, 45, 30, 60}`, how many values satisfy `minutes >= 30`?
questions.explanation: 45, 30, and 60 meet the inclusive threshold, so a correctly updated counter ends at 3.

questions.prompt: Why is `for (std::size_t i = 0; i <= sessions.size(); ++i)` unsafe when the body accesses `sessions[i]`?

options.label: The first iteration skips index zero and begins one position too late
The final iteration uses index `size()`, which is one past the last element
`size()` returns the vector capacity rather than its current element count
The loop becomes unsafe only when `size()` is larger than the maximum value of `int`

questions.explanation: A non-empty vector’s last valid index is `size() - 1`; an empty vector has no valid index. The loop must continue only while `i < sessions.size()`.

questions.prompt: Why should the analyzer compute `total`, `average`, and `longest` as values before composing the report?

options.label: It makes each calculation independently checkable before presentation
It guarantees a fractional average even when both operands remain integers
It prevents later display formatting from changing any calculated value type
It makes a second validation pass over every original input unnecessary

questions.explanation: Named intermediate results can be traced and tested against expected values. Presentation then consumes already-established results instead of hiding several operations in one expression.

questions.prompt: Which set gives the strongest evidence for a study-session analyzer?

options.label: A mixed vector and the same values in reverse order, but no size boundary
Three non-empty vectors with equal totals but no empty or single-element case
A normal mixed vector, a single-element vector, and the explicitly handled empty case
Only the empty case and one maximum-size vector, with no normal expected summary

questions.explanation: Mixed data exercises accumulation and comparison, one element tests initialization, and empty input verifies the guarded precondition instead of division by zero.

skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A function only reads a potentially large module vector. Which parameter avoids copying while preventing mutation through the parameter?

options.label: `const std::vector<int>& credits`
`std::vector<int> credits`
`std::vector<int>& credits`
`std::vector<int>* credits`

questions.explanation: A const reference aliases the caller’s vector without making a full copy and does not permit the function to modify it through that reference.

questions.prompt: Which interface most directly communicates that a function computes and produces a total from a read-only vector?

options.label: `void totalCredits(std::vector<int>& values, int& answer)`
`std::vector<int>& totalCredits(int values)`
`int totalCredits(const std::vector<int>& values)`
`void totalCredits()`

questions.explanation: The return type names the produced result, while the const-reference parameter states the read-only input. This keeps the basic contract explicit.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `const PlanSummary& makePlan(...) { PlanSummary result{/*...*/}; return result; }`?

options.label: Returning a const reference forces the caller to modify `result`
The reference would outlive the local `result` destroyed when the function returns
A local class value cannot be initialized inside a function body
The return statement copies `result`, so the reference always names the caller's copy

questions.explanation: The local `result` is destroyed when the function ends, leaving a returned reference dangling. Returning `PlanSummary` by value gives the caller an owned result whose lifetime is valid.

questions.prompt: For a small `planner` library, which organization supports use from `main.cpp` without duplicating definitions?

options.label: Put function bodies independently in every `.cpp` file
Put only calls in `planner.hpp` and declarations in README
Include `planner.cpp` from every source file
Put the declarations in `planner.hpp` and ordinary definitions in `planner.cpp`

questions.explanation: The header exposes the interface; one source file owns the ordinary definitions. Each consumer includes the header and the linker combines the compiled units.

questions.prompt: The header declares `int total_credits(...)` inside `namespace campus`. Which call names that function explicitly from `main.cpp`?

options.label: `campus.total_credits(credits)`
`campus::total_credits(credits)`
`namespace(total_credits, credits)`
`total_credits::campus(credits)`

questions.explanation: The scope-resolution operator names the function within `campus`. This avoids placing the course library’s names into the global namespace.

questions.prompt: `main.cpp` calls a function defined in `planner.cpp`. Which direct build command supplies both translation units and creates `planner.exe` in the project root?

options.label: `g++ -std=c++20 main.cpp -o planner.cpp`
`main.cpp + planner.cpp > planner.exe`
`g++ planner.hpp -run main.cpp`
`g++ -std=c++20 main.cpp planner.cpp -o planner.exe`

questions.explanation: Both implementation files must be compiled and linked into the same executable. A header supplies declarations but is not a substitute for the source containing the definition.

questions.prompt: Each `.cpp` file compiles, but the final build reports an undefined reference to `totalCredits`. What does that most strongly suggest?

options.label: The caller must include the same guarded header a second time before the linker can find the function
The source-file order on the direct `g++ main.cpp planner.cpp` command must be reversed
The declaration was visible, but a matching definition was not supplied to the link
The executable output name must match the missing function name before linking can succeed

questions.explanation: Successful compilation of the caller means it saw a usable declaration. The linker still needs one matching definition among the compiled translation units.

questions.prompt: The header declares `int totalCredits(const std::vector<int>&);` but the source defines `double totalCredits(std::vector<int>);`. Why can the caller still fail to link?

options.label: The definition does not match the function declared in the header
The compiler uses the return type to select the by-value definition for the const-reference declaration
Value and const-reference parameters always identify the same function, regardless of their declarations
Including the header in the source automatically rewrites the definition to match the declaration

questions.explanation: The definition must match the declaration’s function identity and contract. A by-value parameter is a different overload, and return type alone cannot reconcile the mismatch.

questions.prompt: For `remaining_credits(int target, int completed)`, why are the two `int` parameters reasonable by-value inputs in this course?

options.label: By-value parameters are needed because the function must keep both inputs after it returns
By-value parameters avoid every copy, while reference parameters would copy both integers
Changes to a by-value parameter update the caller only after the function returns
The function receives small independent values and cannot mutate the caller through those parameters

questions.explanation: Small integer copies are ordinary and inexpensive here. By-value parameters also make it clear that local changes do not modify the caller’s original integers.

questions.prompt: Which check best demonstrates that `Module Planner Library` works as a reusable unit?

options.label: Compile `planner.cpp` alone and treat a clean compile as full integration proof
Include the header, link the implementation, call known inputs, and compare results
Run `main.cpp` without linking `planner.cpp` and inspect only editor diagnostics
Include `planner.cpp` directly in `main.cpp` and run one unchecked example

questions.explanation: A consumer-style check tests the exposed declarations, linked definitions, and observable results together without bypassing the library boundary.
