skillCheck.title: Classes, Objects, and Value Ownership Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A `campus::Equipment` value requires a nonblank label and a nonnegative total, and its available count must begin equal to total. Why should its constructor require the label and total?

options.label: Constructor validation means `borrow_one()` and `return_one()` never need to check a transition
Passing the label by value automatically prevents blank text and negative totals
Every successfully constructed object begins with the stated invariant already true
A default object followed by setter calls is equally safe because no code can observe it between those calls

questions.explanation: Construction is the first invariant boundary: it rejects an invalid label or total and initializes available from total, so no successfully created `Equipment` is partly initialized.

questions.prompt: Inside `namespace campus`, which definition directly initializes `label_`, `total_`, and `available_` so a new `Equipment` begins with all stock available?

options.label: `Equipment::Equipment(std::string label, int total) { label_ = label; total_ = total; available_ = total; }`
`Equipment::Equipment(std::string label, int total) : label_{label}, total_{total}, available_{total} {}`
`Equipment::Equipment(std::string label, int total) : label_{label}, total_{total}, available_{0} {}`
`Equipment::Equipment(std::string label, int total) : label_{label}, total_{available_}, available_{total} {}`

questions.explanation: The member-initializer list constructs the owned label and both counts directly. Initializing available from the supplied total establishes the required starting stock state.

questions.prompt: `available_` must always remain between zero and `total_`. Which class design best protects that rule?

options.label: Make both counts public and ask callers to compare them before each assignment
Return a non-const reference from `available()` so callers can repair the count directly
Provide a public `set_available(int)` that assigns any requested count without checking it
Keep the counts private and make `borrow_one()` and `return_one()` reject impossible transitions before mutation

questions.explanation: Private counts prevent bypassing the rule. The two named operations centralize the boundary checks and change available only after the requested transition proves valid.

questions.prompt: The class declares `label_`, then `total_`, then `available_`, but a constructor writes `: available_{total}, total_{total}, label_{label}`. Which member is initialized first?

options.label: `label_`, because members initialize in declaration order
`available_`, because it appears first in the written initializer list
`total_`, because the integer parameter is evaluated before the string
All three initialize simultaneously before the constructor body

questions.explanation: C++ initializes members in declaration order: label, total, then available. Writing the initializer list in that same order makes the real behavior clear and avoids reorder warnings.

questions.prompt: `campus::Equipment projector{"Projector", 1};` receives `projector.return_one()` before any borrow. Which result matches the class contract?

options.label: Increase both total and available to 2 so the returned item can be stored
Return normally without changing state because repeated returns are treated as success
Increase available to 2, then throw after the invariant has been broken
Throw `std::logic_error("all items are already returned")` and leave the object at 1/1

questions.explanation: At 1/1, every item is already available. `return_one` checks that boundary before mutation, throws the exact documented failure, and preserves the valid state.

questions.prompt: A `campus::Equipment` contains `std::string label_`. What happens to that string’s storage when an automatic `Equipment` object leaves scope?

options.label: The string member is destroyed with its object and releases its own resources
A custom destructor must call `delete[]` on `label_.c_str()`
The label buffer remains allocated until program exit because member storage has a separate lifetime
A vector holding the object owns the label buffer separately and releases it only during reallocation

questions.explanation: `std::string` owns and releases its storage through RAII. Destroying the containing `Equipment` automatically destroys the label, so this value type needs no raw allocation or custom cleanup.

questions.prompt: `campus::Equipment original{"Camera", 2};` is copied into `practice_copy`, then `practice_copy.borrow_one()` succeeds. What should the two available counts be?

options.label: Both are 1 because an ordinary class copy aliases the original fields
The original is 1 and the copy is 2 because member calls on a copy are redirected to the source
The original remains 2 and the copy becomes 1 because each value owns its copied fields
Both remain 2 because copied value objects cannot be changed

questions.explanation: The copied string and integers belong to a distinct `Equipment` value. Borrowing from `practice_copy` changes only its available count; the original remains at 2/2.

questions.prompt: `campus::Equipment camera{"Camera", 0};` receives `camera.borrow_one()`. Which result matches the class contract?

options.label: Decrement available to -1, then throw so the caller can inspect the failed value
Throw `std::logic_error("no item is available")` and leave the object at 0/0
Increase total to 1 automatically, then borrow the newly created item
Leave available at 0 but report a successful borrow by clamping the result

questions.explanation: Borrowing at zero is an invalid transition. The method checks first, throws the exact documented failure, and preserves the previously valid total and available counts.

questions.prompt: Which collection matches the loan-desk requirement for three independently owned `campus::Equipment` values without raw `new` or `delete`?

options.label: `std::vector<campus::Equipment>`
`std::vector<campus::Equipment*>` filled with separate `new` calls
`std::vector<std::string>` containing only each object’s current `status_line()` text
One `campus::Equipment` object repeatedly relabelled for all three records

questions.explanation: A vector of values owns each `Equipment` element and manages element lifetime automatically. Each record keeps independent label and stock values without a separate pointer-ownership policy.

questions.prompt: Which check set gives the strongest evidence for the `Equipment Loan Desk` contract?

options.label: Run one successful borrow and infer that construction, return, failure, and copy behavior also work
Compare only `status_line()` output for valid objects and assume private transition rules are correct
Exercise the public methods but accept any exception type or message and omit state checks after rejection
Check the normal transition, all four exact construction/transition failures with unchanged state, and the copy-independence case through public methods

`found == std::vector<Member>::iterator{}`
`found == members.end() - 1`

questions.explanation: Standard range algorithms return that same container’s end iterator as the not-found sentinel. A default-constructed singular iterator is not a substitute for `members.end()` and should not be compared as though it belonged to the range.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm directly counts members whose points satisfy a supplied threshold predicate?

options.label: `std::find`
`std::reverse`
`std::count_if`
`std::copy`

questions.explanation: `std::count_if` applies a predicate across the range and returns how many elements satisfy it.

questions.prompt: `targetId` is a local integer used only for comparison inside a search predicate. Which capture makes that dependency explicit without exposing every local variable?

options.label: `[&]` — every used local by reference
`[=]` — every used local by value
`[]` — no outside local values
`[targetId]` — only that key by value

questions.explanation: Capturing `targetId` by value names the predicate’s only external dependency and gives the predicate its own stable copy. Broad default captures hide which surrounding values the lambda actually uses.

questions.prompt: Which predicate checks whether each `Member` has the requested ID when `targetId` is captured?

options.label: `[targetId](const Member& member) { return member.id() == targetId; }`
`[](Member member) { return targetId; }`
`[member](targetId) { return true; }`
`[&](const Member&) { targetId = 0; }`

questions.explanation: The algorithm supplies each element as the lambda parameter, while the explicit value capture supplies a stable copy of the search key. Returning the equality result gives the required boolean predicate.

questions.prompt: `counts` is a `std::map<std::string, int>`. What does `++counts[member.course()]` accomplish?

options.label: It requires the course key to exist; otherwise the operation fails without changing the map
It increments a temporary integer copy, so the stored count never changes
It inserts a missing course with one but leaves every existing course count unchanged
It inserts zero when missing, then increments that course’s count

questions.explanation: `operator[]` value-initializes an absent mapped integer to zero and returns access to that course’s count, which the prefix increment raises by one.

questions.prompt: A report should check whether a course key exists without adding it. Which approach avoids the insertion behavior of `operator[]`?

options.label: `counts[course] == 0` only
`counts.find(course) != counts.end()`
`++counts[course]`
`counts.clear()`

questions.explanation: `find` searches without changing the map. Using `operator[]` on a missing key creates an entry, which would mutate a supposedly read-only report.

questions.prompt: The required order is points descending, then name ascending when points match. Which comparator implements that complete strict rule?

options.label: `if (left.points() != right.points()) return left.points() > right.points(); return left.name() > right.name();`
`if (left.points() != right.points()) return left.points() >= right.points(); return left.name() <= right.name();`
`if (left.points() != right.points()) return left.points() > right.points(); return left.name() < right.name();`
`if (left.points() != right.points()) return left.points() < right.points(); return left.name() < right.name();`

questions.explanation: Higher points must compare first; tied points fall back to lower name. Both comparisons are strict, so an element never compares before itself.

questions.prompt: A ranked display is needed, but the original roster must remain in insertion order. Which plan satisfies both requirements?

options.label: Bind `auto& ranked = roster`, then sort `ranked`
Use `std::stable_sort` directly on `roster` because stable sorting never changes container order
Sort `roster`, then copy the already sorted values into `ranked`
Copy `roster` into `ranked`, then sort only `ranked`

questions.explanation: A value copy gives the ranked view independent element order. Sorting the copy changes only `ranked`; an alias or any sort applied to `roster` changes the canonical collection.

questions.prompt: The roster needs uppercase display names while preserving each stored `Member::name()`. Which plan satisfies that contract?

options.label: Create a destination name vector sized to the roster, then use `std::transform` to write uppercase copies into it
Call `reserve(roster.size())` on an empty destination, then write through `destination.begin()`
Transform into the original roster and rely on a later sort to restore the original names
Create one output string and overwrite it for every member, then treat that final string as the complete display list

questions.explanation: A correctly sized destination gives `std::transform` valid output positions. Producing uppercase copies there preserves the canonical names while making the display conversion explicit.

skillCheck.title: File Streams, Failure Preservation, Debugging, and Checks Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: After `inspect_regular_file` has confirmed that `data/revisions.txt` exists and is a regular file, which sequence correctly begins reading its records?

options.label: Read the entire input loop first and check only `eof()` afterward
Create `std::ofstream output{"data/revisions.txt"};`, check it, and then try to read records from it
Default-construct an input stream, call `getline`, and open the file only after that read fails
Create `std::ifstream input{"data/revisions.txt"};` and check `if (!input)` before reading

questions.explanation: An input file stream attempts to open the named file during construction. Its state must be checked before any extracted data is trusted.

questions.prompt: Which loop makes each full text record available for parsing, including fields that may contain spaces?

options.label: `while (!input.eof()) { input >> line; }`
`for (line : input) {}`
`while (std::getline(input, line)) { /* parse line */ }`
`while (output << line) {}`

questions.explanation: `getline` returns the stream, whose condition succeeds only when a complete read succeeds. It preserves spaces and avoids processing a stale value after a failed read.

questions.prompt: A stored revision record requires exactly `id|topic|minutes`. A line has only `id|topic`. What should the loader do?

options.label: Classify the line as malformed rather than accepting a partial record
Reuse the minutes field from the previous record
Treat the missing minutes as zero and accept the record
Keep the ID and topic as a partial record to complete during a later save

questions.explanation: The line does not contain all three fields required by the persisted record contract. Silently supplying or reusing minutes would manufacture state that the file did not contain.

questions.prompt: How should a first launch with no `data/revisions.txt` differ from a file that exists but contains an invalid record?

options.label: Both must be reported as successful loads of one empty record
Missing may start empty; malformed existing data must fail without being accepted
The malformed file should be treated as a normal first run
Both should erase all in-memory state

questions.explanation: Absence can be an expected initial condition. Existing but malformed content is evidence of a persistence problem and needs an explicit failure path.

questions.prompt: Why load and validate all lines into a temporary vector before assigning them to the tracker’s current records?

options.label: Clear current records before parsing so old and new data can never mix
Assign each parsed line directly, then roll back the live vector if a later line fails
Any malformed line can fail the load before current valid state is replaced
Keep the valid prefix and ignore the first malformed line

questions.explanation: A staged load separates validation from commitment. The program changes its live state only after the full candidate data set has proved acceptable.

questions.prompt: The tracker opens an output stream successfully but a later write fails. What evidence should determine whether save is reported as successful?

options.label: The filename contains `.txt`
The stream remains good after the complete write and close/flush path
At least one insertion operator was attempted
The old file existed before launch

questions.explanation: Opening is only the first step. The stream state after the required output operations reveals whether the complete record set was actually written successfully.

questions.prompt: One stored record causes the loader to reject a file. What is the strongest first debugging approach?

options.label: Run the full file and place breakpoints across several parser branches before isolating the record
Change the parser delimiter and writer format together, then see whether the failure disappears
Repair the line before saving its original text or expected result, then rerun the full file
Keep one failing line, record expected versus actual, then trace its parse

questions.explanation: A minimal reproducible input anchors the investigation. Comparing expected and actual behavior supports one causal repair and a meaningful rerun.

questions.prompt: A breakpoint stops immediately after splitting a record line. Which inspection most directly tests the suspected field-count defect?

options.label: The input line and parsed fields at that breakpoint
Only the output file after the program has already exited
Only the candidate value, without the input line or parsed fields
Only the current source line, without inspecting any program values

questions.explanation: Those values show what entered the parser and what it produced at the precise failing step. They can confirm or disprove the field-count hypothesis.

questions.prompt: What is the essential behavior of the supplied `check_equal(label, actual, expected)` helper?

options.label: Print expected and actual but always return success so the remaining checks run
Compare values, label any mismatch, and make the check command fail
Replace expected with actual after the first failure so later reruns are green
Stop on the first mismatch without printing its label or expected value

questions.explanation: A credible check preserves the independent expectation, exposes a diagnostic difference, and makes the overall command fail when a required behavior is wrong.

questions.prompt: A checked candidate exists, the helper has renamed the known-good live file to `.bak`, and candidate-to-live promotion now fails. What must happen before the operation returns?

options.label: Delete `.bak` so the next save starts without conflicting recovery data
Report success because the candidate was completely written before promotion
Restore `.bak` to the live path, report the failed promotion, and do not claim a successful save
Open the missing live path with truncation and rebuild it from whichever records remain in memory

questions.explanation: The backup is retained specifically until candidate promotion succeeds. On failure, restoring it to the live path preserves the last known-good bytes; the operation must still report that the requested save failed.

templates.label: tracker.hpp interface
Exact interactive application contract
templates.content:
One launch may add at most one revision.
1. Load data/revisions.txt before prompting. On any unusable or invalid existing data: print `ERROR: stored revision data is invalid or unavailable; no changes were written.` and return 1.
2. Display each loaded line as `#<id> <topic> - <minutes> minutes`; if empty print `No revisions recorded.`
3. Prompt `Topic (blank to exit): `. A blank/whitespace-only line prints `No changes written.` and returns 0 without saving. A topic longer than 60 or containing | prints `ERROR: topic must be 1-60 characters and contain no |.` and returns 1 without saving.
4. Prompt `Minutes (1-600): ` and parse the complete line. Failure or an out-of-range value prints `ERROR: minutes must be a whole number from 1 to 600.` and returns 1 without saving.
5. add_revision rejects capacity with `ERROR: tracker capacity of 30 reached.` and maximum ID with `ERROR: no revision ID remains.`; either result returns 1 without saving.
6. Save only the successful new state. Save failure prints `ERROR: revision data could not be saved; previous data was preserved.` and returns 1. Success prints `Saved revision #<id>.` and returns 0.

Normal proof: add Vectors review / 45, exit, restart, and show the same ID plus next-ID behavior. Rejected-add proof: preserve exact live bytes before and after one invalid topic or minutes case.

skillCheck.title: Integrate, Verify, and Publish a C++ CLI Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: Before reading `argv[1]` as the command, which condition must the CLI establish?

options.label: `argc >= 2`
`argc >= 1`, because index 1 always exists after the program name
`argv[1] != nullptr`, checked before confirming that index 1 exists
`argc == 1`, because the program name is not included in the count

questions.explanation: `argc` counts the program name as the first argument. At least two entries are required before index 1 denotes a supplied command.

questions.prompt: A learner runs `coursepilot.exe` without a command. What response best preserves a clear CLI contract?

options.label: Treat the missing command as bare `list` and return success
Show usage but return success, making the invalid invocation indistinguishable from `help`
Load and rewrite storage unchanged before reporting the missing command
Show usage and return a nonzero status without changing data

questions.explanation: Usage text makes the repair path visible, while a nonzero status lets scripts and reviewers distinguish invalid invocation from success.

questions.prompt: The supported commands are `add`, `list`, `complete`, `summary`, and `help`, but the user enters `archive`. What should happen?

options.label: Treat `archive` as an undocumented alias for `complete`
Report it, show usage, and leave stored records unchanged
Report the unknown command but still rewrite the current records before returning failure
Accept it as a no-op success so scripts can continue without an error

questions.explanation: An unsupported command has no valid state transition. Explicit rejection and usage guidance avoid surprising mutation or undocumented behavior.

questions.prompt: `complete` accepts exactly one record ID after the command. Which condition must dispatch verify before reading that ID?

options.label: `argc >= 2`, because seeing the command token is sufficient
`argc >= 3`, so extra trailing arguments are accepted
`argc == 3`, counting the program name, command, and exactly one ID
`argc == 2`, counting only the program and command

questions.explanation: Requiring exactly three arguments proves that the ID position exists and rejects both missing and unexpected extra arguments before any indexed access.

questions.prompt: The `complete` command receives an ID that does not exist. What should happen to the persistent records?

options.label: Create a completed record with that unknown ID
Leave them unchanged, report the rejected operation, and do not run the save path
Replace the file with an empty one
Partly modify the first record as a fallback

questions.explanation: No valid transition exists, so there is no new state to persist. Keeping both memory and disk unchanged protects the existing records.

questions.prompt: Which README instruction gives a reviewer the most reproducible verification path from the project root?

options.label: Name only an editor Run task without its starting folder or expected output
Give a compiler command but omit the check command and expected observations
Give exact build/check commands plus CLI examples and expected results
Provide only a screenshot of a successful run without reproducible commands

questions.explanation: Exact starting location, commands, and expected observations let another person repeat the build and checks without depending on hidden editor state.

questions.prompt: Which paths should normally be ignored while `.cpp`, `.hpp`, checks, and README remain tracked?

options.label: Build output: `out/`, `*.o`, and `*.exe`
Every `.hpp` file plus the `out/` directory
All files under `data/`, including the tracked `.gitkeep`, but no compiler outputs
Only debug executables whose names end in `-debug.exe`

questions.explanation: Object files and executables are reproducible build products. Source, headers, checks, and documentation are the reviewable inputs needed to recreate them.

questions.prompt: Why inspect `git status --short` both before and after staging `CoursePilot`?

options.label: To compare file modification times and prove the executable was rebuilt after every edit
To confirm that a successful local commit has already been copied to the remote repository
To verify ignored files are absent without checking whether any were tracked or staged earlier
To see exactly what changed and what would enter history before committing

questions.explanation: The two status views expose unstaged and staged paths, giving the learner a chance to remove generated output, credentials, or private records.

questions.prompt: A real learner-records file appears in the staged list. What should happen before the commit?

options.label: Commit it, delete it in the next commit, and assume deletion removes it from history
Leave it staged but add a matching ignore rule before committing
Unstage it, add an ignore rule or safe sample, then recheck status
Rename the file generically while keeping its real contents staged

questions.explanation: Sensitive data must not enter repository history. Correcting and rechecking the staged set is safer than attempting to remove exposed history afterward.

questions.prompt: The local checks pass and the push succeeds. What final action gives the strongest human-reviewable handoff evidence?

options.label: Assume a successful push proves every behavior
Fresh-clone, follow README, run checks and CLI cases, then inspect saved results
Run only the old executable in the original working folder
Add untested features directly on the remote

questions.explanation: A clean-clone verification tests whether tracked source, multi-file build instructions, checks, CLI contract, and persistence behavior are sufficient for another person.

builds.title: CoursePilot CLI
builds.outcome: A persistent CoursePilot executable with add, list, complete, summary, and help commands, ten passing checks, defensive storage, an honest README, and a clean GitHub repository verified from a fresh clone.
builds.brief: Build `CoursePilot`, a dependency-free C++20 command-line study-task tracker. Use `main.cpp`, `task.cpp/.hpp`, `store.cpp/.hpp`, the unchanged Week 7 `file_ops.hpp`, and `checks.cpp`. Commands are exactly `add <course> <title>`, `list [open|done|all]` with omitted filter meaning all, `complete <id>`, `summary`, and `help`; there is no command-line data-path option. Persist runtime data at `data/tasks.txt` as `id|status|course|title`; allow OPEN/DONE only, IDs 1..1,000,000, and at most 100 tasks. Reject missing/extra arguments, blank or delimiter-containing fields, invalid or exhausted IDs, repeated completion, capacity overflow, duplicate IDs, and malformed existing storage before any write. List results are always ID-ascending and summary course keys are alphabetic. Use the supplied exact success/error messages, checked candidate replacement, standard algorithms/map, and no raw allocation. The live `data/tasks.txt` remains ignored and the tracked empty data directory is represented only by `data/.gitkeep`.

steps.text: Create the supplied tracked tree; copy the unchanged Week 7 `file_ops.hpp`; then copy the record grammar, argc/argv/result table, exact messages, build commands, ten-check list, README headings, `.gitignore`, and acceptance cases before implementation. Assign each rule to StudyTask, TaskService, TaskStore, or main.

Implement StudyTask construction and completion invariants plus TaskService add/find/filter/sort/complete/summary behavior through value-owned vectors, algorithms, narrow lambdas, and map counts. Produce list copies in ID-ascending order and summary course counts in map-key order.

Implement TaskStore load and candidate replacement by reusing the copied Week 7 helper unchanged with full record, capacity, duplicate, and ID-range validation; only a confirmed missing first-run file begins empty, and runtime state remains at ignored `data/tasks.txt`.

Implement command routing from the supplied table: validate exact argc before every argv read, fully parse IDs, make bare `list` equivalent to `list all`, keep help independent of storage, reject every unlisted shape, emit the exact result/error message, and return the documented success/failure status.

Write ten dependency-free checks for first/next/maximum ID, blank/delimiter fields, list filter/order, valid complete, missing/repeated complete no-mutation, summary counts, malformed preservation, and save/restart.

Run normal, empty, boundary, invalid, restart, malformed, and rollback-related acceptance cases; seed one non-strict comparator or next-ID defect, reproduce one focused check, inspect it in the debugger, repair one cause, and rerun all checks.

Finish README prerequisites, UCRT64/VS Code setup, exact release/debug/check commands, command examples, storage/recovery, architecture, ordering, known limits, and troubleshooting; use fictional values only in documentation and never stage the live tasks file.

Initialize Git, inspect status before and after staging, prove `data/tasks.txt` is ignored and `data/.gitkeep` is tracked, make focused local commits, create an empty GitHub repository, push normally, clone to a fresh folder, follow only README commands, rerun checks/cases, and inspect the published file list.

acceptanceCriteria.text: Every listed command shape matches the supplied argc/argv table before an argument is read; missing, extra, or unknown forms emit the exact error plus usage, return failure, and perform no write.
Task construction and completion preserve all field/status/ID invariants; capacity or ID exhaustion and every invalid operation produce the exact error without mutation or arithmetic overflow.
Bare `list` means all; explicit open/done/all results are ID-ascending, and summary uses status totals plus alphabetic map-key course counts without changing canonical stored state.
Valid data survives restart, while malformed existing data, a stale backup, candidate-promotion failure, and failed service operations leave the live file unchanged through the copied Week 7 helper.
All ten named checks and the complete acceptance table pass after one recorded debugger-led repair.
The supplied commands build the application and check executable warning-clean from a fresh Windows clone, and the README reproduces those commands exactly.

The public repository contains intended source, `file_ops.hpp`, checks, README, ignore rules, and `data/.gitkeep`, but no `data/tasks.txt`, executable/object output, secrets, editor machine paths, or real learner records.

hints: Treat each listed command as an explicit grammar; argc is part of that grammar and there is no optional data-path argument.
Check capacity and `highest_id < 1000000` before addition; save only after a service operation returns a successful new state.
Inspect staged paths because .gitignore does not unstage a file already added; verify `git check-ignore data/tasks.txt`.

templates.label: Record grammar and ordering
templates.content:
id|status|course|title
- id: whole number 1..1000000 and unique
- status: OPEN or DONE
- course: nonblank; no | or newline
- title: nonblank; no | or newline
- capacity: 100 tasks
- next ID: highest + 1 only when highest < 1000000; otherwise reject without adding or writing
- list output: matching tasks sorted by ID ascending
- summary output: OPEN/DONE totals, then course counts in alphabetic map-key order
- live path: data/tasks.txt (ignored; never publish)

templates.label: Complete command and argument table
templates.content:
| Invocation | argc | argv after program name | Result | May write? |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| .\coursepilot.exe | 1 | none | invalid-command error + usage; failure | no |
| .\coursepilot.exe help | 2 | help | usage; success | no; do not load storage |
| .\coursepilot.exe add "CSC 101" "Revise vectors" | 4 | add, course, title | Added task #<id>. | yes, after validation |
| .\coursepilot.exe list | 2 | list | same as list all | no |
| .\coursepilot.exe list open | 3 | list, open | OPEN tasks by ascending ID or No tasks found. | no |
| .\coursepilot.exe list done | 3 | list, done | DONE tasks by ascending ID or No tasks found. | no |
| .\coursepilot.exe list all | 3 | list, all | all tasks by ascending ID or No tasks found. | no |
| .\coursepilot.exe complete 1 | 3 | complete, id | Completed task #1. | yes, only on success |
| .\coursepilot.exe summary | 2 | summary | status totals, then alphabetic course counts | no |
| unknown command/filter, missing or extra argument | varies | unlisted shape | invalid-command error + usage; failure | no |

PowerShell requires the .\ prefix for a local executable. There is no command-line data-file-path argument. Validate argc before each argv access.

templates.label: Exact result and error contract
templates.content:
Success/output:
- Added task #<id>.
- Completed task #<id>.
- No tasks found.
- list line: #<id> [<OPEN|DONE>] <course> - <title>
- summary first line: OPEN: <n> | DONE: <n>
- summary course line: <course>: <n>

Errors (print exactly, then return failure):
- ERROR: invalid command. Run .\coursepilot.exe help.
- ERROR: id must be a whole number from 1 to 1000000.
- ERROR: task not found.
- ERROR: task is already complete.
- ERROR: course and title must be nonblank and contain no | character.
- ERROR: task capacity of 100 reached.
- ERROR: no task ID remains.
- ERROR: stored task data is invalid; no changes were written.
- ERROR: task data could not be saved; previous data was preserved.

templates.label: Exact build and check commands
templates.content:
# Release application
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.cpp task.cpp store.cpp -o coursepilot.exe

# Debuggable dependency-free checks
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -g checks.cpp task.cpp store.cpp -o coursepilot-checks.exe
.\coursepilot-checks.exe
$LASTEXITCODE
